title: Amphotericin B (mucormycosis): monitor potassium and magnesium (renal toxicity)
vignette: A 54-year-old man comes to the hospital due to 4 days of progressive nasal congestion, facial pain, swelling, and fever. The patient has taken over-the-counter decongestants, which provided no relief. He has a history of uncontrolled diabetes mellitus due to dietary and medication noncompliance. Temperature is 38.3 C (101 F). Examination shows right facial swelling and purulent nasal discharge with necrotic destruction of the nasal mucosa and turbinates. The diagnosis of invasive mucormycosis is made, and surgical debridement is performed. He is started on an antifungal agent that binds to ergosterol and alters cell membrane permeability. Considering the adverse effects of this medication, which of the following should be routinely monitored in this patient?

clues.note: Invasive mucormycosis (in poorly controlled diabetes) is treated with amphotericin B - the antifungal that binds ergosterol.

clues.text: binds to ergosterol and alters cell membrane permeability
clues.note: An antifungal that binds ergosterol to form membrane pores is a POLYENE - amphotericin B, whose major toxicity is renal (with potassium and magnesium wasting).

whatMatters: An ergosterol-binding antifungal = AMPHOTERICIN B (a polyene). Its most notorious toxicity is NEPHROTOXICITY, which causes renal potassium and magnesium WASTING - so serum POTASSIUM and MAGNESIUM must be routinely monitored (and repleted). Answer D.
strategy: Identify amphotericin B (ergosterol binder), then recall its adverse effects: renal toxicity (vasoconstriction + direct tubular injury -> HYPOkalemia and HYPOmagnesemia, renal tubular acidosis, azotemia) and infusion reactions (fever/chills - 'shake and bake'). Monitor potassium and magnesium (and renal function). Reject platelet count (heparin/beta-lactams), calcium (bisphosphonates/foscarnet), creatine phosphokinase (daptomycin - rhabdomyolysis), and TSH (amiodarone/lithium).

eliminations.label: Platelet count - heparin/beta-lactams/vancomycin
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: monitoring for thrombocytopenia (heparin, beta-lactams, vancomycin). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: isolated thrombocytopenia is not the characteristic amphotericin B toxicity; electrolyte/renal monitoring is. ✅ Correct if: drugs causing thrombocytopenia.

eliminations.label: Serum calcium - bisphosphonates/foscarnet
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: monitoring for hypocalcemia (bisphosphonates, foscarnet). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: amphotericin's hallmark is potassium/magnesium wasting, not primarily calcium. ✅ Correct if: bisphosphonate/foscarnet-related hypocalcemia.

eliminations.label: Creatine phosphokinase - daptomycin (rhabdomyolysis)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: monitoring CPK for rhabdomyolysis (daptomycin, statins). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: amphotericin B does not cause rhabdomyolysis. ✅ Correct if: daptomycin/statin myopathy.

eliminations.label: Thyroid-stimulating hormone - amiodarone/lithium
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: TSH monitoring for thyroid dysfunction (amiodarone, lithium). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: amphotericin B does not affect the thyroid. ✅ Correct if: amiodarone or lithium therapy.

reasoning: An ergosterol-binding antifungal is amphotericin B (a polyene)
Its most notorious adverse effect is renal toxicity (vasoconstriction + tubular injury)
Renal injury causes potassium and magnesium wasting (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia)
-> routinely monitor serum potassium and magnesium; answer D
mechanism: Amphotericin B is a POLYENE antifungal that binds ERGOSTEROL in the fungal cell membrane, forming pores that increase membrane permeability and cause cell death; it is the initial drug of choice for serious invasive mycoses such as MUCORMYCOSIS. Its most notorious adverse effect is RENAL TOXICITY: it causes renal arteriolar vasoconstriction (reducing GFR) and a direct toxic effect on tubular epithelial cells, producing acute tubular necrosis, renal tubular acidosis, and electrolyte disturbances - characteristically HYPOKALEMIA and HYPOMAGNESEMIA from increased distal tubular losses (often requiring daily repletion), plus azotemia and a normochromic normocytic anemia (reduced erythropoietin). Therefore serum POTASSIUM and MAGNESIUM (and renal function) should be routinely monitored. Amphotericin also causes acute infusion reactions (fever, chills, rigors - 'shake and bake'). Liposomal formulations reduce nephrotoxicity. The distractors are monitoring parameters for other drugs: platelets (heparin/beta-lactams), calcium (bisphosphonates/foscarnet), CPK (daptomycin), and TSH (amiodarone/lithium).

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Pharm > amphotericin B: polyene, binds ergosterol -> membrane pores; nephrotoxicity (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, RTA, azotemia, anemia), infusion reactions ('shake and bake'); monitor K/Mg + renal function.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Ergosterol binder = amphotericin B -> renal K/Mg wasting -> monitor potassium and magnesium.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on amphotericin B, polyene, ergosterol, nephrotoxicity, or renal tubular acidosis? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Platelets (heparin), calcium (bisphosphonates/foscarnet), CPK (daptomycin), TSH (amiodarone/lithium) are other drugs' monitoring.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: amphotericin B -> nephrotoxicity with hypokalemia + hypomagnesemia; monitor K/Mg + creatinine; 'shake and bake' infusion reaction.

firstAid.detail: Pharm: nephrotoxicity -> hypokalemia + hypomagnesemia; monitor K/Mg + renal function.

memoryHook: Amphotericin B is 'ampho-terrible' for the kidneys - it flushes out potassium and magnesium, so keep checking (and refilling) K and Mg.
